I would keep it simple and stay with the crop pattern I know best in Quzhou: winter wheat followed by summer maize on the same land. Around here that is the steady road, it matches our water, our machines, and the local habit of farming. At 70, I would not spread myself into too many crops like cotton or vegetables, because they need more watching, more labor, and more risk. I would rather run one familiar grain rotation well than chase a higher price and lose sleep over it. I would use improved wheat seed and hybrid maize seed, keep fertilizer moderate instead of pushing too hard, irrigate wheat more than maize because spring is dry here, and hold pesticide sprays to only the key timings. For tillage, I would no-till or direct-seed maize after wheat harvest to save time and moisture, then use rotary tillage before wheat sowing in autumn. I would aim for solid, realistic yields, not demonstration-field yields, because on my own farm I care more about stable harvest and manageable work than record output. This matches the local Quzhou wheat-maize system reported by China Agricultural University’s Quzhou station and its county demonstrations: https://qzsyz.cau.edu.cn/art/2024/2/25/art_46232_1012984.html and https://qzsyz.cau.edu.cn/art/2024/10/8/art_46317_1039835.html
